{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=functional+self-awareness+architectures+epistemic+self-correction+assumptions&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1093/9780197851708.003.0007\", \"title\": [\"Self-Aware Believing and Epistemic Akrasia\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n                  <jats:p>This chapter argues that self-awareness will sometimes lead to cases of what is often thought of as rational epistemic akrasia. These are cases where subjects are rational to have a belief, while simultaneously rationally believing that they are not rational to have that belief. It concentrates on a certain kind of akrasia that can be induced by taking higher-order evidence seriously: examples where akratic subjects are rational to expect accuracy and rationality to diverge in their own cases. Using these cases, the chapter rejects arguments for the impossibility of rational akrasia. It also rejects some formal principles that would allow some degree of akrasia, but would place general limits on it. And it rejects the suggestion that akratic beliefs manifest some defect in the subject who has them.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197851708.003.0007\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 9, 11]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1093/9780197851708.003.0006\", \"title\": [\"Self-Aware Believing and Epistemic Dilemmas\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n                  <jats:p>This chapter argues that taking rational account of self-awareness results in “epistemic dilemmas.” These are cases in which rational requirements conflict with one another. The chapter discusses two kinds of strategies for avoiding dilemmas in our theory of rationality. The first avoids dilemmas by separating normative notions. The second avoids dilemmas by postulating indeterminacy about rationality. The chapter rejects both sorts of moves, in part by arguing that neither strategy avoids what might seem most troubling about dilemmas. It then argues that admitting dilemmas should not be seen as a problem. Instead, epistemic dilemmas should be seen as a natural and expectable consequence of rational self-awareness, and of taking HOE seriously.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197851…

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=cognitive+reasoning+agents+incident+reporting+industrial+safety+automated+analysis&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.5220/0007518105830588\", \"title\": [\"Patient Safety Incident Reporting Analysis Based on Integrity and Commitment Team in Inpatient\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.5220/0007518105830588\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2017]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.58837/chula.the.2024.453\", \"title\": [\"Classification dental patient safety incidents and creating a dental incident reporting system model from an academic dental hospital's incident reporting data\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Background: Underreporting of adverse events (AEs) in dentistry hinders patient safety and quality improvement. The Dental Incident Reporting System (DIRS) was developed to address this gap, integrating a comprehensive classification system and user-centered design to enhance reporting accuracy and usability. Methods: This mixed-methods study involved: (1) Developing a classification system using 752 incident reports, validated by experts. (2) Designing DIRS with input from dental professionals and heuristic evaluations by IT experts. (3) Conducting usability testing with 16 participants using the System Usability Scale (SUS) and User Acceptance Test (UAT). Results: The classification system covered 28 categories of dental AEs, aligning with national standards and enabling structured reporting. DIRS achieved a SUS score of 69.69, indicating above-average usability. UAT results showed high ratings for effectiveness (3.15), usefulness (3.15), and satisfaction (3.38). Participant experience had no significant impact on ratings, highlighting DIRS's accessibility across diverse user groups. These results support the broader applicability of DIRS in various dental healthcare settings. Conclusions: DIRS facilitates comprehensive AE documentation and enhances patient safety and risk management. Iterative refinements, guided by expert feedback and usability testing, significantly improved data entry efficiency and report generation. Most common steps in such cycle involve- recognizing a problem, defining it, developing a strategy in order to fix it, organizing knowledge and resources available, monitoring progress, and evaluating the effectiveness of the solution. Once a solution is obtained, another problem usually comes, and the cycle starts again. Searching techniques in problem-solving by using artificial intelligence (A.I) are surveyed in this paper. An overview of definitions, development and dimensions of A.I in the light of search for solutions to problems are accepted. Dimensions as well as relevance of search in A.I research is reviewed. A classification of searching in the matter of depth of known parameters of search was also investigated. At last, the forethoughts of searching in AI research are brought into prominence. Search is noticed that it is the common thread that binds most of the problem-solving strategies in AI together.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.…
